items.stem: A team wants the chatbot to answer from the latest internal docs that change weekly. The most appropriate first approach is:

options.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the current docs
options.rationale: Correct: RAG injects fresh, changing knowledge without retraining.

options.text: Fine-tune the base model nightly on all docs
options.rationale: Costly and slow for weekly-changing content; RAG is the standard choice.
Does not scale and goes stale immediately.
Temperature controls randomness, not knowledge freshness.

items.explanation: Correct: RAG injects fresh, changing knowledge without retraining.

items.stem: Which TWO practices help control the cost of an LLM feature? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Cache responses for repeated or similar requests
options.rationale: Correct: caching avoids paying for identical generations.

options.text: Route easy requests to a smaller/cheaper model
options.rationale: Correct: model routing matches cost to difficulty.

options.text: Always send the full conversation history every call

options.rationale: Removing evals does not reduce inference cost and harms quality.

items.explanation: Correct: caching avoids paying for identical generations.

items.stem: Why is 'LLM-as-judge' evaluation used with caution?

options.text: The judge model can be biased or inconsistent, so it needs calibration and human spot-checks
options.rationale: Correct: automated judges are useful but must be validated against human labels.
It is not; it can share the generator's blind spots.

options.text: It removes the need for any eval set
options.rationale: You still need curated eval data.

options.text: It only works for image models
options.rationale: It is used for text generation evaluation.

items.explanation: Correct: automated judges are useful but must be validated against human labels.
